d7mCmgUSKk4.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 4: Self-Purification (Tazkiyah)
d7mCmgUSKk4.one_line: Tazkiyah is one of the four objectives of prophethood and a third of the deen: understand and govern your nafs, do deeds well and sincerely, control only yourself.
d7mCmgUSKk4.summary: The sheikh argues that self-purification is a fundamental, not a specialist extra. In the Quran Allah lists four objectives of every prophet: teaching who Allah is, purifying people, teaching the law and teaching the wisdom to apply it, and He moved tazkiyah from Ibrahim's last place to second. Half of what prophets bring is therefore ethics and the inner life. The pre-Islamic Arabs had boundless pride; Islam tuned it into healthy self-assurance and humility, and the Prophet corrected arrogance sharply. He poses three questions: what is your plan if your deeds are rejected; why were you given freedom of choice, if not to overcome the inner obstacles between knowing right and doing it; and why does Allah reward physical acts that do not benefit Him, unless He is looking at the heart. Islam has three domains, practice, theology and ihsan, and each deserves a third of one's learning. Ihsan means doing things well and sincerely, which people value even without religion. The nafs, which never ages, is not the enemy but a cheerleader that must be understood and tamed. The only thing you may try to control is yourself; controlling others breeds manipulation, and education changes behaviour better than bans. Tazkiyah is a path walked for life, not a destination.

outline.heading: Islam is built on clear fundamentals
outline.gist: The most important matters come first and most often in the Quran; over centuries every faith drifts into disputed details and loses its basics.

outline.heading: Self-evident maxims of the deen
outline.gist: Last year's Reduced Concepts and this series point to things the Prophet never needed to explain; yesterday's fiqh session contained nothing disputed.

outline.heading: Interlude
Showing that tazkiyah is fundamental
outline.gist: Tonight's aim is not to teach the topics of tazkiyah but to show it is a critical, neglected part of Islam.

outline.heading: A process, not perfection
outline.gist: Self-awareness matters even without religion; the faith has three domains and believing you can become perfect is itself a disease.

outline.heading: Why and how you act matters: the plumber
outline.gist: Even a simple repair job is judged by manners, attitude and quality; Allah likewise cares about the inner side of deeds.

outline.heading: The four objectives of prophethood and their order
outline.gist: Ibrahim's prayer put purification last; in Allah's replies it moves to second, showing the order matters.

outline.heading: Objective one: who Allah is
outline.gist: The universe shows a single, knowing, capable, purposeful creator, but His mercy, justice and forgiveness are known only through revelation.

outline.heading: Objective two: purifying the self
outline.gist: We understand the world yet not what is inside our own ribcage; the claim that Shaytan can take over the driver's seat would mean the Quran missed something vital.

outline.heading: Objective three: the book of law
outline.gist: Once you know Allah and yourself, the rulings tell you what to do.

outline.heading: Objective four: the wisdom to apply it
outline.gist: A ruling applied in the wrong setting backfires; extremism is law without wisdom.

outline.heading: Half the prophetic mission is ethics and the inner life
outline.gist: Theology, tazkiyah, fiqh and wisdom map to four disciplines; zakat given with humiliation fails its purpose.

outline.heading: The Arabs: proud of nothing
outline.gist: With no wealth, government or book they were proud of their camels, sand and lineage, which made them good material once tempered.

outline.heading: Self-value as a rare elixir
outline.gist: You can reduce excess confidence but cannot easily buy it; those with low self-esteem take long to fill the void.

outline.heading: Islam tuned their pride into humility
outline.gist: Walk humbly on the earth; the companions began competing in service, and the Prophet corrected any boast of superiority directly.

outline.heading: Always question yourself
outline.gist: We expect Islam to fit our views; tazkiyah means constantly asking whether you are doing right, with healthy self-assurance.

outline.heading: Question one: what if your deeds are rejected?
outline.gist: Imagine some 150,000 prayers handed back; there is no plan B, and the Quran shows rejection is more likely than we admit.

outline.heading: Question two: why do we have freedom of choice?
outline.gist: Animals cannot regulate themselves, as livestock eat until they die; humans can choose what they do not want for a longer-term good.

outline.heading: Freedom means overcoming the struggle within
outline.gist: Right and wrong take five minutes to explain; the nafs, Shaytan and desire stand between knowing and doing.

outline.heading: Question three: why reward acts that do not benefit Allah?
outline.gist: Unlike Greek myths where offerings feed the gods, nothing we do strengthens Allah.

outline.heading: Allah looks at hearts
outline.gist: Like a parent touched by a child's clumsy offer to help, what matters to Allah is the intention, love and care behind the act.

outline.heading: Solutions lie in the opposite direction
outline.gist: We look outward for answers that lie within; you choose whether your nafs drowns, drifts or excels.

outline.heading: Three domains: this is simply Islam, not Sufism
outline.gist: People object that he is turning Sufi, yet Jibril's three questions define the religion.

outline.heading: Practice: worship Him as He wants
outline.gist: Learn fiqh thoroughly; worshipping God my way is not an option.

outline.heading: Theology: where we stand in the story
outline.gist: Iman explains why we are here, what is expected and what follows.

outline.heading: Ihsan: the nafs never ages
outline.gist: The body changes beyond recognition but the inner self stays the same child; he has seen dying men in their nineties still eyeing nurses.

outline.heading: Fifty mistakes is a pattern; laziness is a made-up word
outline.gist: We cannot explain why we repeatedly do what we regret; the Quran explains what laziness and other states really are.

outline.heading: Regret and the common human experience
outline.gist: Harsh bosses later wish they had been better; anyone, religious or not, can benefit from asking why.

outline.heading: Give ihsan a third of your learning
outline.gist: Traditional schools taught the three domains with tools like language and logic before specialisation.

outline.heading: Ihsan is doing things well: be reliable
outline.gist: Sloppy people are a burden; he calls himself not the smartest doctor but reliable, and reliability makes you employable.

outline.heading: We are sensitive to people's gain
outline.gist: Gratitude fades when we discover a helper had an angle; people treasure sincerity.

outline.heading: Sincerity is the door to the Divine
outline.gist: Allah gains nothing physically, so He looks only at sincerity; ihsan connects the finite to Him, so balance it with fiqh and theology.

outline.heading: Control nothing but yourself
outline.gist: Trying to control others causes harm; educate, encourage, mentor and model instead, whether as parent, teacher or imam.

outline.heading: Controllers end up manipulating
outline.gist: Those obsessed with control live unhappily and resort to lies or force; children will make their own choices as you did.

outline.heading: Education beats bans: tobacco
outline.gist: Legal bans on smoking failed, while graphic packaging, advertising limits and school campaigns cut smoking sharply.

outline.heading: Marijuana needs education, not just law
outline.gist: Bans failed and it was legalised; real change needs sustained education about its harms.

outline.heading: Islamic penalties came last
outline.gist: Hudud were revealed late, after the ethical norm was established; law protects norms rather than creating them.

outline.heading: Your nafs is your cheerleader, not your enemy
outline.gist: It loves you but does not know what is good for you; tame it and it becomes an ally, while Shaytan is the real enemy.

outline.heading: Why it matters: well-intended people are safe
outline.gist: People without hidden agendas are trusted and easy to be around.

outline.heading: Marry the humble and compassionate
outline.gist: Humble, compassionate people make lasting marriages, friendships and workplaces; value them before leaving.

outline.heading: High standards make people reliable
outline.gist: Those who hold themselves to high ethics are professional and loyal.

outline.heading: Self-critical people grow
outline.gist: Criticism directed inward drives improvement; directed outward it exhausts everyone, though self-criticism must not destroy self-value.

outline.heading: Inner peace keeps you grounded in reality
outline.gist: People at peace with themselves are stable, unlike those who lose their grasp of reality as they age.

outline.heading: Non-Muslims can attain some self-regulation
outline.gist: Everyone has a nafs and spirit; others can reach spirituality and self-control, but not the full sincerity and humility that knowing Allah brings.

outline.heading: What tazkiyah gives a Muslim
outline.gist: Ethical consistency, humility, courage, control of one's choices and mindfulness of the present moment.

outline.heading: Joy in prayer and peace with death
outline.gist: Connection with Allah in every salah, and accepting mortality and accountability.

outline.heading: The journey, not the destination
outline.gist: Tazkiyah is spiritual striving: keep questioning yourself, repenting and trying harder, a path that continues even in Paradise.

outline.heading: Outro

0WPA4B7pNi0.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 25: The Significance of the Quran
0WPA4B7pNi0.one_line: Three verses on the Quran: the command to reflect on it, reminding with it without coercion, and its unanswered challenge to produce anything like it.
0WPA4B7pNi0.summary: On the twenty-fifth night he insists that a Muslim cannot be whole without a real connection to the Quran, which is why the full Quran should be heard at least once in Ramadan. He then explains three verses. From Muhammad 47:24 he separates tadabbur from seeking knowledge: listening to explanations gives information, but only one's own unhurried thought anchors it. Hearts locked by sin and distraction receive nothing, which is why people can read the Quran for years without their habits changing. From Qaf 50:45 he argues that the Prophet was never sent to coerce; forced faith only breeds hypocrisy, so the task is to remind with the Quran. The Quran works on a heart that already takes its mortality seriously, so with some people one must begin with basic existential questions. From At-Tur 52:33-34 he reads the challenge as a ladder: bring a way of life like it, then a book, ten surahs, one surah, then something only somewhat like it. He closes with Musaylimah's failed imitation and a follower who admitted tribal loyalty was the only reason. He asks listeners to use the last five nights to reflect deeply and attach themselves to at least one ayah.

outline.heading: Why the whole Quran must be heard in Ramadan
outline.gist: He defends completing the Quran in taraweeh at least once and says a Muslim without a felt connection to the Quran has a missing link in his deen.

outline.heading: Interlude
Surah Muhammad and the command to reflect
outline.gist: He introduces Surah Muhammad as one of the surahs about the Prophet and reads the question: will they not reflect on the Quran?

outline.heading: Tadabbur is not the same as seeking knowledge
outline.gist: Hearing a sheikh or reading translations is learning; tadabbur is sitting with an ayah and asking what it means to you and how you live it.

outline.heading: Reflection anchors what you learn
outline.gist: Information that is not reflected on drifts away like an unanchored boat; the Prophet made seclusion and contemplation part of his worship all year.

outline.heading: The sister verse: no contradiction in the Quran
outline.gist: The parallel verse in An-Nisa says a book from anyone but Allah would be full of inconsistencies, while the Quran explains and reinforces itself.

outline.heading: Locks on the heart
outline.gist: A heart covered with sin and distraction cannot receive Allah's light; even a good insight is a gift from Allah, not one's own credit.

outline.heading: Reflection cleans the heart and changes behaviour
outline.gist: Contemplation acts like chlorine on the heart and produces the desire to do good; when nothing goes in, habits never change.

outline.heading: Five nights left: attach yourself to one ayah
outline.gist: Scarcity makes the last nights precious; one verse that moves you deeply is enough, as the Prophet would repeat a single verse all night.

outline.heading: The Prophet delivered the Quran intact
outline.gist: He ensured it was written, memorized and recited even in the rhythm he recited it, so that we could reflect on it.

outline.heading: Surah Qaf and the slander of Quraysh
outline.gist: Qaf tells the story of existence, death, resurrection and reward; its last verse comforts the Prophet as Quraysh attack his character and the Quran.

outline.heading: You are not a compeller over them
outline.gist: Jabbar means one who coerces; the Prophet's role, and ours, is to remind, teach, model and encourage.

outline.heading: Forced faith breeds hypocrisy
outline.gist: Coercion produces people who perform religion for the perks and drag communities down; Allah could have forced belief but made it a choice with consequences.

outline.heading: Strive against disbelief with the Quran
outline.gist: Linking to Al-Furqan, he says the Quran is the tool to challenge people's arguments and choices.

outline.heading: Guidance belongs to Allah
outline.gist: You cannot guide whom you love; Allah guides whoever wills to be guided. He notes the dropped letter in 'my warning'.

outline.heading: The Quran works on a heart that fears the warning
outline.gist: Only someone who has thought about death and accountability benefits; with others, begin with existential questions about why they exist and where they are going.

outline.heading: The nafs resists the consequences, not the narrative
outline.gist: People admire the Islamic way of life but do not want its cost; the heart must fear Allah's warning before the reminder works, and the Quran is all the reminder needed.

outline.heading: The accusation that he made it up
outline.gist: Within a run of challenging questions in At-Tur, Allah asks whether they claim the Prophet invented the Quran, then challenges them to bring a hadith like it.

outline.heading: First challenge: a hadith means a whole way of life

ODPGnyEiLwQ.one_line: Reviving dead hearts: Ibrahim ibn Adham's ten reasons duas go unanswered, taken one at a time.
ODPGnyEiLwQ.summary: On the twenty-second night of Ramadan 2025 the single reminder between the rakaat is about reviving dead hearts. The speaker compares these nights to the shock a defibrillator gives a heart that has stopped: sometimes the spiritual heart needs a jolt to beat again. He tells how Shaqiq al-Balkhi asked Ibrahim ibn Adham why people call on Allah, who promised to answer, and are not answered. Ibrahim replied that their hearts had died in ten things, and the speaker takes them one at a time: knowing Allah without giving Him His due, perhaps the weightiest; reading the Quran without acting on it; claiming to love the Prophet while leaving his sunnah; calling Shaytan an enemy while agreeing with him; wanting Paradise without working for it; fearing the Fire while walking into it; affirming death without preparing for it; being busy with others' faults and blind to one's own; consuming Allah's blessings without thanking Him; and burying the dead without learning from them. He recalls Abu Bakr telling people at prayer time to rise and put out the fire they had lit, and asks everyone to assess honestly the state of his heart, since a person can walk around alive with a dead heart, and these nights are the time to revive it.

outline.heading: Fifth: loving Paradise without working for it
outline.gist: They said they love Paradise and did not work for it, though the wise one is he who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death.

outline.heading: Sixth: fearing the Fire while walking into it
outline.gist: They said they fear the Fire yet handed themselves over to it; Abu Bakr would tell people at prayer time to rise and put out the fire they had lit, and we need to be that serious with ourselves.

outline.heading: Seventh: affirming death without preparing for it
outline.gist: They said death is true, and every soul will taste it, yet did not prepare.

outline.heading: Eighth: busy with others' faults, blind to your own
outline.gist: They occupied themselves with their brothers' faults and threw their own behind their backs.

outline.heading: Ninth: consuming blessings without thanks
outline.gist: They ate from their Lord's blessings and did not thank Him for them.

outline.heading: Tenth: burying the dead without learning from them
outline.gist: They buried their dead and took no lesson; each of the ten is a shock meant to bring hearts back to life.

outline.gist: Each person needs to assess deeply the state of his heart, because one can walk around alive while the heart is dead; these nights are the time for its revival.

f5PLMSzQDRU.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 16: Sincerity vs Ostentation
f5PLMSzQDRU.one_line: Ikhlas as the inner mirror of tawhid, the two roots of riya, and how sincerity arrives as the fruit of the whole tazkiyah path.
f5PLMSzQDRU.summary: He defines ikhlas simply: doing something only for the reason you claim to be doing it, with no hidden secondary gain. It is the inward reflection of tawhid, the condition for any deed to be accepted, and something Allah grants rather than something we manufacture; our part is lifelong striving toward it. Its opposite, riya, is craving status in people's hearts, and he traces it to two roots. The first is the nafs believing that other people's admiration will make you stronger and safer; the cure is constant magnifying of Allah until you see that people are as weak and lost as you are, like drowning people clinging to each other. The second is a lack of self-value that makes you need validation; the cure is grounding your worth in Allah, though he stresses that children must receive real attention growing up or they will crave it as adults, and fame only deepens the void. He warns against the nafs's trick of seeking sincerity so that people will love you. Ikhlas and khushoo come late, as results of earlier work: daily contemplation to build focus, and speaking to Allah as your real self without the social mask. He closes by urging everyone to keep private deeds that no one will ever know, illustrated by Ali Zayn al-Abidin's secret night charity.

outline.heading: Opening
Ikhlas defined: doing a thing only for its stated reason
outline.gist: Sincerity is simple in definition: act for the purpose you claim and add no hidden motive or secondary gain.

outline.heading: Our built-in sense for insincerity
outline.gist: People can feel when someone has an ulterior motive; this sensor protects us from betrayal and heartache.

outline.heading: Ikhlas as the inner reflection of tawhid
outline.gist: Tawhid is the outward claim and ikhlas is its mirror in the heart, which is why the surah that describes Allah's oneness is named Al-Ikhlas.

outline.heading: Ikhlas is granted, our job is to strive for it
outline.gist: No one achieves sincerity by effort alone; Allah bestows it, and our duty is lifelong vigilance and work toward it, asking for it in prayer.

outline.heading: The condition for acceptance and the hidden shirk
outline.gist: Allah accepts no deed shared with a partner; the shirk the Prophet feared most is hidden, subtler than an ant on a rock at night.

outline.heading: Riya: craving status in people's hearts
outline.gist: Ikhlas is the sum of all the tazkiyah values; to approach it, understand its opposite, ostentation, which is more complex because it has two roots.

outline.heading: First root: the nafs thinks people can make you strong
outline.gist: The nafs wants your survival and power and believes others' admiration and respect will give you food, protection and command.

outline.heading: Second root: craving attention from low self-value
outline.gist: Without stable self-worth you need others to keep validating you; the fix is understanding your value as divinely given and fixed.

outline.heading: Children need attention to grow stable
outline.gist: Self-sufficient worth requires a childhood with enough loving attention; deprived children keep craving it as adults.

outline.heading: Crave Allah's attention instead of people's
outline.gist: Knowing Allah sees and hears you and is pleased with you should become more meaningful than anyone else's gaze.

outline.heading: Why ikhlas is taught later, not to young children
outline.gist: Children understand the world by impressing visible people; as they mature the balance shifts from external validation to inner worth.

outline.heading: Fame as a drug that widens the void
outline.gist: The more attention one gets, the more one needs; once-famous people sink into depression when the applause stops.

outline.heading: Magnifying Allah cures the belief that people can help you
outline.gist: Constant exalting of Allah trains the self to see that people are as weak as you, like drowning people clinging to each other.

outline.heading: The nafs's trick: be sincere so people will love you
outline.gist: Seeking sincerity so that Allah makes people admire you returns you to the same problem; only Allah's approval is the goal.

outline.heading: Ikhlas is a late result, not a starting point
outline.gist: Sincerity comes naturally once self-value, humility, love and other foundations are in place, which is why the series reached it now.

outline.heading: Khushoo as attending to the one you speak to
outline.gist: Like a conversation where one partner keeps texting someone else, prayer without focus offends; khushoo is being fully present with Allah.

outline.heading: Khushoo: an emotional response to a mental acceptance
outline.gist: Khushoo is the heart's response to the clear conviction that there is nowhere better to be than this prayer; tears are not the measure.

outline.heading: Daily contemplation builds the focus khushoo needs
outline.gist: Months of daily reflection yield only a minute of clarity; Ramadan moments of focus fade because the problem is inside, not the imam.

outline.heading: Sincerity means the real you speaks to Allah
outline.gist: Take off the social mask of title and status when addressing Allah; keep it with people, but speak to Him as your weak true self.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr weeping as he led the prayer
outline.gist: Abu Bakr could not hold back his tears in prayer because he never addressed Allah as anyone other than who he was.

outline.heading: Allah already knows who you are
outline.gist: Formality with Allah makes no sense when He sees everything you have done; speak to Him honestly and khushoo follows.

outline.heading: Keep secrets between you and Allah
outline.gist: Ikhlas is a secret even angels cannot record; keep some deeds no one, not even family, will ever learn of.

outline.heading: Ali Zayn al-Abidin's secret night charity
outline.gist: Scars found on his back at his washing were explained only when the poor complained that the nightly sacks of food left at their doors had stopped.

outline.heading: The nafs will resist private worship at first
outline.gist: Alone at night the nafs will hope someone sees you, but persistence lets Allah's pleasure replace the craving for admiration.

outline.heading: Outro

XYCa0tvp-mk.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 2: Conspiracy Theories
XYCa0tvp-mk.one_line: A balanced Muslim approach to conspiracy theories: where they come from, what they do to us, and the Quranic answer of accountability, vigilance and organization.
XYCa0tvp-mk.summary: Part of a series refocusing Muslims on fundamentals, this talk takes on conspiracy thinking, which feeds the same craving for the outrageous that makes people know controversies before they know their prayer. His thesis: of course enemies conspire, and we must be aware and prepared, but plots are human, not divine decree, and cannot be blamed for our own failures. He traces conspiracy theories to four sources: discomfort with ignorance, which makes us fill gaps; a felt powerlessness that Shaytan cultivates; laziness about learning how complex the world really is, worsened by social media flattening the old hierarchy of earned authority; and real conspiracies, which do exist. Using Nero's rumoured survival, vaccines and his oncology patients, he shows how holes in a narrative are exploited and how such beliefs shape behaviour, and he notes the same pattern in religious superstition about jinn. The real payoff of conspiracy thinking is evading accountability, and enemies spread such theories to drain morale, as attempted after Gaza. The Quranic response is self-accountability, identifying real enemies, and organizing efforts, modelled by the Prophet's intelligence network and refusal to complain. He ends with a call for Muslims to earn political representation and a seat at the table.

outline.heading: Back to fundamentals
outline.gist: The series aims to refocus Muslims on the basics rather than controversies and details.

outline.heading: Only the outrageous gets attention
outline.gist: His clips that spread were outrageous-sounding snippets; people who say outrageous things usually have an agenda other than education.

outline.heading: Craving controversy over basics
outline.gist: Young Muslims who cannot pray properly know Aisha's age and hand amputation, showing the self's craving for sensational information.

outline.heading: A balanced approach
outline.gist: Conspiracy thinking has grown as never before, and he wants neither to dismiss nor to swallow it.

outline.heading: The thesis: enemies conspire, but plots are not decree
outline.gist: We must be aware and prepared, and we cannot blame conspirators for our own mistakes and shortcomings.

outline.heading: Stories born of ignorance and powerlessness
outline.gist: A quoted author notes we invent stories when ignorant and powerless, assuming the world is far more organized than it is.

outline.heading: If there is a cabal, it is not doing well
outline.gist: Any group plotting against us is losing ground.

outline.heading: First source: ignorance
outline.gist: We oppose what we do not understand and, uncomfortable with not knowing, fill the void with made-up conclusions.

outline.heading: Being comfortable saying 'I don't know'
outline.gist: Not content with ignorance of what benefits us, but stable without knowing.

outline.heading: Filling in the gaps about people
outline.gist: We reduce strangers to a word; assume the best unless your role makes you responsible for vigilance.

outline.heading: The Illuminati and a halted lecture
outline.gist: An audience once stopped this lecture to prove a conspiracy, proving his point.

outline.heading: Second source: powerlessness
outline.gist: You are never powerless while breathing; the feeling is Shaytan's illusion that leads to complaining instead of acting, as many felt after October 7.

outline.heading: The next generation acted
outline.gist: Encampments, posting and advocacy moved public opinion even without changing the reality.

outline.heading: Change by millimetres
outline.gist: One life may move things a millimetre; hundreds of millions doing so is real change, so do not equate small impact with none.

outline.heading: Third source: laziness
outline.gist: Accepting an easy theory spares the effort of learning how complex and contested the world is.

outline.heading: Beliefs become behaviour
outline.gist: Beliefs shape values, attitudes and actions, so lazy beliefs cause real harm; seek people with knowledge.

outline.heading: Social media flattened earned authority
outline.gist: Speaking once required years of service and favour; now anyone with a camera is heard.

outline.heading: Generosity and courage once made chiefs
outline.gist: Leadership used to cost wealth and risk; now lying boldly can win a presidency.

outline.heading: Fourth source: real conspiracies
outline.gist: Everyone has plotted against someone; some theories are true, but not at today's scale.

outline.heading: Neither credulous nor naive
outline.gist: Governments do not tell everything, as parents do not; avoid both believing everything and believing nothing.

outline.heading: Nero and the dead who never die
outline.gist: Rumours of Nero's survival lasted decades, like Elvis and Tupac.

outline.heading: Why: better safe than sorry
outline.gist: Fear makes people prefer a belief that keeps their guard up despite contrary evidence.

outline.heading: Vaccines as a medical miracle
outline.gist: Obstetric care, antibiotics and vaccines grew the population to eight billion, though every medicine has side effects.

outline.heading: A hole in the narrative
outline.gist: Failing to admit rare severe reactions hands conspiracy theorists a hole they make their sole focus.

outline.heading: The mindset matters more than the claim
outline.gist: Whether 9/11 was a conspiracy is not his concern; the reasoning behind such beliefs is.

outline.heading: Expert critique is healthy
outline.gist: Specialists critiquing a vaccine improve it; non-experts drawing conclusions from unverifiable sources do harm.

outline.heading: Suspicion in the oncology clinic
outline.gist: Patients accuse him of serving big pharma and bring obscure studies, while unexplained remissions are studied rather than mythologized.

outline.heading: Conspiracy thinking in religion and climate
outline.gist: A whole sect believes parts of the Quran were hidden, and some still call global warming a plot.

outline.heading: Certainty versus vigilance
outline.gist: Do not be sure of a conspiracy; acknowledge the possibility, stay alert, and test claims from all sides with trusted experts.

outline.heading: The payoff: evading accountability
outline.gist: Blaming a powerful group spares us from admitting mediocrity and mistakes.

outline.heading: Conspiracy theories as a weapon
outline.gist: Enemies spread despairing theories to drain morale, as tried after Gaza, but the students held their ground.

outline.heading: Superstition is the religious equivalent
outline.gist: Jinn and evil eye are real but nowhere near what people believe; no patient asks if a liver spot is a jinn.

outline.heading: Their plots are human; plot back
outline.gist: Ignoring conspiracies shows weakness, but believing they always succeed defeats us from within.

outline.heading: Quranic answer 1: self-accountability
outline.gist: The self-critical are slower to believe others are to blame and quicker to fix their own failures.

outline.heading: Quranic answer 2: know your enemies
outline.gist: Shaytan, declared oppressors, hypocrites and even enemies at home, each handled differently, some with pardon.

outline.heading: Quranic answer 3: organize your efforts
outline.gist: Scattered sheep are easy prey; like the ants in A Bug's Life, weakness is often within.

outline.heading: The Prophet's intelligence network
outline.gist: He knew of caravans and armies in advance and planned for them, never naive.

outline.heading: He built instead of complaining
outline.gist: When Quraysh blocked him, he sought other tribes and a new city; human plotters do not control outcomes, Allah does.

outline.heading: The need for political representation
outline.gist: Not a replica of the early caliphate, but a united front that speaks for Muslims.

outline.heading: A microphone in your face
outline.gist: Without a shared narrative, Muslims are cornered with loaded questions.

outline.heading: Earn a seat at the table
outline.gist: No one gives a seat for free; it is easy to plot against someone absent, so support people entering every field and school board.

outline.heading: If you cared, you would be there
outline.gist: Forty thousand people without a single representative should stop pretending to care.

outline.heading: What conspiracy thinking does to morale
outline.gist: Choosing between bad options and being betrayed follows from absence; the real damage is lost grit and initiative.

outline.heading: A fire kindled in the next generation
outline.gist: The pain of the last fifteen months has shown young people they can make change if they persist.

2pqcMJTfvmk.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 22: Submissions
2pqcMJTfvmk.one_line: Three forms of submitting free will to Allah: Ibrahim and Ismail obeying the command, Dawud admitting his mistake, and the heart melting at the Quran.
2pqcMJTfvmk.summary: He explains that Islam literally means submission, and that Allah gave humans free will, something even angels lack, precisely so that they could surrender it by choice. That choice carries great risk and great reward, and submitting to no one unconditionally except Allah frees a person from every other master; the Giver of free will knows best how to use it. That is why the whole faith carries the name Islam. His first example is Ibrahim and Ismail in 37:103-107: a command with no secondary gain, against every instinct, carried out without knowing the outcome until the knife struck, which he contrasts with the Eid sacrifice, a reminder that Allah aligns our submission with our own good. The second is Dawud in 38:21-25, who on his half day of worship answered intruders politely yet ruled without hearing the other party, then repented without excuses; he draws from it that we answer for our own wrongs, not others', and should not use eloquence to win what is not ours. The third is spiritual submission in 39:23, where the skins and hearts of those who revere Allah soften into His remembrance on hearing the Quran.

outline.heading: Islam means submission
outline.gist: Islam, surrender and peace share one root; the literal meaning is submitting your will to Allah.

outline.heading: Free will given to be submitted
outline.gist: The paradox: Allah grants free will and then asks you to surrender it, the difference being that you do so consciously and by choice.

outline.heading: Angels cannot comprehend desire
outline.gist: They have no urge to sin and could no more grasp it than we could a sixth sense; humans can say no, as three weeks of fasting with food at hand proves.

outline.heading: The trust of free will: risk and reward
outline.gist: Free will is the rarest thing in creation; misusing it is dangerous, but surrendering it by choice earns an experience beyond what other creation is offered.

outline.heading: Submit to no one unconditionally but Allah
outline.gist: Any other authority over you exists only by your consent, as with the law or parents; this frees you from the shackles of a consumerist existence.

outline.heading: Its Giver knows best how to use it
outline.gist: Why learn to use free will from others who merely received it? The margin of choice is small, but use it well and Allah grants a far wider will.

outline.heading: A reward beyond imagination
outline.gist: Paradise holds what no eye has seen or mind imagined; like Allah's mercy, it is described in terms we grasp only partly.

outline.heading: Why the whole faith is named Islam
outline.gist: Practice is one part alongside belief and inner purification, yet the name for all of it is Islam because submitting free will is the critical piece.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's submission had no secondary gain
outline.gist: Often we gain reputation or a good feeling from obeying, which can threaten sincerity; Ibrahim gained nothing and even his soul resisted.

outline.heading: His only son, in his prime
outline.gist: Not any child but his beloved only son, now a fine young man; no part of the command offered any ease.

outline.heading: The annual sacrifice: commands aligned with our good
outline.gist: Every Eid Muslims slaughter in gratitude that Allah never asked them to harm themselves; we feed family and the poor while Ibrahim was told to slaughter his son.

outline.heading: He did not know the outcome: no bluff
outline.gist: We read it knowing the ending; Ibrahim did not, and Allah let him go step by step until the blade actually struck.

outline.heading: 'When they both submitted': Ismail's side
outline.gist: Left as an infant in the desert and saved by Zamzam, Ismail could have resented his father, yet he too submitted fully.

outline.heading: Facing death young
outline.gist: From treating young cancer patients he knows how hard it is to accept death young; Ismail asked to be laid face down to spare his father, and the sharpened knife would not cut.

outline.heading: The vision fulfilled and the ransom
outline.gist: Allah called out that Ibrahim had fulfilled the vision and ransomed Ismail with a ram struck by the same knife.

outline.heading: Allah made submission easy and we still neglect it
outline.gist: At the coming Eid, reflect that He could have required harmful acts but tied obedience to our interest; praise Him rather than claim you would have done what Ibrahim did.

outline.gist: King, judge, smith, commander and prophet, he reserved half a day for uninterrupted worship; we book time off for leisure, prophets for worship.

outline.heading: The Prophet's private prayer and the start of tarawih
outline.gist: Praying alone behind a screen, he was joined by companions until the masjid filled; he stayed in so that the prayer would not become obligatory.

outline.heading: Voluntary worship as love
outline.gist: Obligations are submission; voluntary acts are love shown to Allah, and the Prophet wanted that option kept for his ummah.

outline.heading: The intruders and the ninety-nine ewes
outline.gist: Two men climbed the wall into his private chamber and posed a dispute: one with ninety-nine took his brother's single ewe.

outline.heading: Dawud's ruling and the test
outline.gist: He held his temper and answered respectfully about partners wronging each other, then realised they were angels testing him and he had erred.

outline.heading: Hear the other side: the judge and the gouged eye
outline.gist: A classical judge refused to rule for a man whose eye had been gouged out until he heard the other party, who might have lost both eyes.

outline.heading: A small mistake, not justified
outline.gist: His slip was understandable, but prophets never rationalise mistakes; Dawud admitted it and fell in prostration, which is why we prostrate at this verse.

outline.heading: 'We forgave him': you answer for yourself
outline.gist: Allah treated it as a real sin; whatever the intruders did, the question is what you did wrong, and others' repentance is not your concern.

outline.heading: Nearness, a good return and the first 'khalifah'
outline.gist: Admitting error earned Dawud closeness to Allah; the companions first heard the word khalifah in this story, before its later mention in Madinah.

outline.heading: Eloquence that wins a piece of the Fire
outline.gist: The Prophet warned that he judges by what he hears, and whoever wins by better argument what is not his receives a piece of Hell; submit to the truth when you know you are wrong.

outline.heading: The best of speech, consistent and paired
outline.gist: Allah sent down the finest words ever spoken, each part reinforcing the rest into one coherent narrative.

outline.heading: Skins that shiver and hearts that soften
outline.gist: Those who revere their Lord feel the Quran on their skin, then skin and heart melt into His remembrance.

outline.heading: Spiritual submission: losing yourself in remembrance
outline.gist: After obeying the command and submitting to the truth comes the soul's surrender, a moment of being part of something greater; this is Allah's guidance, and whom He leaves astray none can guide.

pPNMADz_qpE.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 24: Arrogance and Humbleness
pPNMADz_qpE.one_line: Arrogance as the enemy within and humbleness as seeing reality, through Pharaoh's boast, the knowledgeable one led astray, and two sons at forty.
pPNMADz_qpE.summary: He calls arrogance the inner arch-enemy behind evils such as racism, which he describes as collective arrogance, and warns especially against letting religiosity make one look down on others. Humbleness, he insists, is not low self-esteem but seeing the truth: all humans are equally weak, dealt different hands, and judged by a criterion only Allah knows, so the need to compare reveals unstable self-worth; a believer compares only with his past self. From 43:51-54 he shows Pharaoh, shaken by the magicians' conversion, boasting that the Nile flows beneath him and mocking Musa's speech, only for that water to close over his head; Pharaoh insulted his people's intelligence, they obeyed, and he came to believe his own lies, which is why arrogance that convinces itself is so hard to cure. From 45:23 he warns against shaping God to fit one's desires and against knowledge that breeds arrogance, as with Iblis, urging people to read the Quran as it is. From 46:15-19 he contrasts the man who at forty, at the peak of his strength, turns to Allah in gratitude, with the son who mocks his pleading parents: be humble by choice or life will humble you.

outline.heading: Arrogance and humbleness among the top Quranic themes
outline.gist: Many Quranic stories and teachings target arrogance, the enemy within that every life struggles with, because the ego keeps trying to prove its superiority.

outline.heading: Racism as collective arrogance
outline.gist: Great evils grow from hidden diseases of the heart that surface when we are angry, threatened, tired or failing, and Allah is displeased by them.

outline.heading: A servant with an ego does not know his place
outline.gist: No one with an atom's weight of arrogance enters Paradise, whatever the reason he feels better than others.

outline.heading: Never let religiosity make you look down on others
outline.gist: Using Allah's guidance to feel superior to those still lost, as you once were, is a deal breaker.

outline.heading: Humbleness is seeing the truth, not low self-esteem
outline.gist: We are all weak, controlling neither our arrival nor departure, and the criterion of who is better is known only to Allah.

outline.heading: Everyone was dealt a different hand
outline.gist: You do not know where others started their race, so comparison is apples to oranges.

outline.heading: Stable worth: compare yourself to your past self
outline.gist: The need to compare is a cry of unstable self-worth; Allah has already declared every human valuable, so a believer's worth does not rise and fall with success or sin.

outline.heading: Ask yourself whether you show arrogance
outline.gist: Make humbleness your objective and hold yourself to account even if you attend no lessons, listening to how the Quran exposes this sin.

outline.heading: Pharaoh's rare direct speech after the staff
outline.gist: This is the only place Pharaoh is quoted this way, after Musa's staff swallowed the magicians' illusions.

outline.heading: Interlude
The magicians convert and Pharaoh must respond
outline.gist: His secret weapon prostrated publicly, Musa's credibility soared, and Pharaoh needed a counter-move.

outline.heading: 'Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, with these rivers beneath me?'
outline.gist: His palace was built over the Nile, so it literally ran under his feet.

outline.heading: Words that Allah's decree turns against you
outline.gist: The water beneath his feet would soon close over his head; a boast made in pride or spite can follow you to your grave.

outline.heading: Only Allah is King; what you own is a trust
outline.gist: History's fallen kings show that possessions pass from one owner to the next; nothing is truly yours.

outline.heading: 'Better than this despised one who can hardly speak'
outline.gist: Pharaoh mocked Musa's speech impediment, a cheap blow at something no one controls, like height, weight, colour or birthplace.

outline.heading: Demands for gold bracelets and angels
outline.gist: Physical miracles only invite demands for more; the Prophet's lasting miracle is the Quran, and practising it makes you the miracle.

outline.heading: He belittled their minds and they obeyed
outline.gist: Pharaoh made arguments he knew were absurd and his people accepted them; the scary part is that he came to believe them himself.

outline.heading: Nine signs to peel away self-deception
outline.gist: Allah gave Pharaoh nine signs as chances to strip the layers of lies until he saw he was not divine.

outline.heading: When you believe your own lie
outline.gist: Arrogance you know is wrong can be corrected; arrogance you believe, like calm intellectual racism, cannot be argued away.

outline.heading: Interlude
Letting desire dictate who God is
outline.gist: The verse is not about worshipping desire itself but shaping one's image of God to suit oneself, or inventing a god that does.

outline.heading: Led astray despite knowledge
outline.gist: Knowledge sought for the wrong reason breeds arrogance and becomes a source of misguidance, which is why the Prophet sought refuge from knowledge that does not benefit.

outline.heading: Iblis: knowledge without humility
outline.gist: Iblis knew far more than any of us, yet arrogance festered until he challenged Allah and asked for time to mislead Adam's children.

outline.heading: Sealed hearing and heart, veiled sight
outline.gist: Such a person sees things as he wants them, not as they are, and only Allah can guide him.

outline.heading: Read the Quran as it is, not as you want it
outline.gist: Accept the truth in its totality, including the parts your heart dislikes, and change yourself to love them.

outline.heading: The mother's thirty months of hardship
outline.gist: Life begins, continues and ends in pain, and the mother bears much of it through pregnancy and nursing.

outline.heading: Why forty is the peak of strength
outline.gist: The sum of physical, mental, emotional, financial and social strength peaks around forty, the age of the Prophet's revelation.

outline.heading: At the top of the mountain, look up
outline.gist: At his peak the believer asks for gratitude, righteous deeds, good offspring and repentance; success should make you look up to Allah, not down on people.

outline.heading: Interlude
Their best deeds accepted, their faults forgiven
outline.gist: Such people are promised acceptance and a place in Paradise.

outline.heading: The son who says 'uff' and mocks resurrection
outline.gist: At the same peak another man tells his parents he is sick of them and scoffs that the long-decayed dead could return.

outline.heading: Humble by choice or humbled by circumstance
outline.gist: If you will not choose humility, life, the grave and finally the Day of Judgment will humble you.

outline.heading: Parents forced into humility
outline.gist: He humiliated his parents by leaving them pleading with Allah while he dismissed the promise as ancient myths; such people are the losers.

outline.heading: Degrees for what they did
outline.gist: Everyone receives back what they project: condescend to people and you will be condescended to, and no one is wronged.

outline.heading: Keep the ability to see your own arrogance
outline.gist: He prays for a path of humbleness and the ability to notice and hold oneself accountable for vanity before it becomes a slippery slope.

40:39.ar: يَٰقَوۡمِ إِنَّمَا هَٰذِهِ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا مَتَٰعࣱ وَإِنَّ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَ هِيَ دَارُ ٱلۡقَرَارِ
40:39.en: O my people! Lo! this life of the world is but a passing comfort, and lo! the Hereafter, that is the enduring home

40:40.ar: مَنۡ عَمِلَ سَيِّئَةࣰ فَلَا يُجۡزَىٰٓ إِلَّا مِثۡلَهَاۖ وَمَنۡ عَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوۡ أُنثَىٰ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنࣱ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ يَدۡخُلُونَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ يُرۡزَقُونَ فِيهَا بِغَيۡرِ حِسَابࣲ‏
40:40.en: Whoso doeth an ill-deed, he will be repaid the like thereof, while whoso doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, (all) such will enter the Garden, where they will be nourished without stint

40:41.ar: ۞وَيَٰقَوۡمِ مَا لِيٓ أَدۡعُوكُمۡ إِلَى ٱلنَّجَوٰةِ وَتَدۡعُونَنِيٓ إِلَى ٱلنَّارِ
40:41.en: And, O my people! What aileth me that I call you unto deliverance when ye call me unto the Fire

40:42.ar: تَدۡعُونَنِي لِأَكۡفُرَ بِٱللَّهِ وَأُشۡرِكَ بِهِۦ مَا لَيۡسَ لِي بِهِۦ عِلۡمࣱ وَأَنَا۠ أَدۡعُوكُمۡ إِلَى ٱلۡعَزِيزِ ٱلۡغَفَّٰرِ
40:42.en: Ye call me to disbelieve in Allah and ascribe unto Him as partners that whereof I have no knowledge, while I call you unto the Mighty, the Forgiver

40:43.ar: لَا جَرَمَ أَنَّمَا تَدۡعُونَنِيٓ إِلَيۡهِ لَيۡسَ لَهُۥ دَعۡوَةࣱ فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَلَا فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ وَأَنَّ مَرَدَّنَآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَأَنَّ ٱلۡمُسۡرِفِينَ هُمۡ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِ
40:43.en: Assuredly that whereunto ye call me hath no claim in the world or in the Hereafter, and our return will be unto Allah, and the prodigals will be owners of the Fire

40:44.ar: فَسَتَذۡكُرُونَ مَآ أَقُولُ لَكُمۡۚ وَأُفَوِّضُ أَمۡرِيٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بَصِيرُۢ بِٱلۡعِبَادِ
40:44.en: And ye will remember what I say unto you. I confide my cause unto Allah. Lo! Allah is Seer of (His) slaves

40:45.ar: فَوَقَىٰهُ ٱللَّهُ سَيِّـَٔاتِ مَا مَكَرُواْۖ وَحَاقَ بِـَٔالِ فِرۡعَوۡنَ سُوٓءُ ٱلۡعَذَابِ
40:45.en: So Allah warded off from him the evils which they plotted, while a dreadful doom encompassed Pharaoh's folk

41:6.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ بَشَرࣱ مِّثۡلُكُمۡ يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَيَّ أَنَّمَآ إِلَٰهُكُمۡ إِلَٰهࣱ وَٰحِدࣱ فَٱسۡتَقِيمُوٓاْ إِلَيۡهِ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرُوهُۗ وَوَيۡلࣱ لِّلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ
41:6.en: Say (unto them O Muhammad): I am only a mortal like you. It is inspired in me that your Allah is One Allah, therefor take the straight path unto Him and seek forgiveness of Him. And woe unto the idolaters

41:13.ar: فَإِنۡ أَعۡرَضُواْ فَقُلۡ أَنذَرۡتُكُمۡ صَٰعِقَةࣰ مِّثۡلَ صَٰعِقَةِ عَادࣲ وَثَمُودَ
41:13.en: But if they turn away, then say: I warn you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt (which fell of old upon the tribes) of A'ad and Thamud

41:33.ar: وَمَنۡ أَحۡسَنُ قَوۡلࣰ ا مِّمَّن دَعَآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَعَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا وَقَالَ إِنَّنِي مِنَ ٱلۡمُسۡلِمِينَ
41:33.en: And who is better in speech than him who prayeth unto his Lord and doeth right, and saith: Lo! I am of those who are muslims (surrender unto Him)

5:3.ar: حُرِّمَتۡ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡمَيۡتَةُ وَٱلدَّمُ وَلَحۡمُ ٱلۡخِنزِيرِ وَمَآ أُهِلَّ لِغَيۡرِ ٱللَّهِ بِهِۦ وَٱلۡمُنۡخَنِقَةُ وَٱلۡمَوۡقُوذَةُ وَٱلۡمُتَرَدِّيَةُ وَٱلنَّطِيحَةُ وَمَآ أَكَلَ ٱلسَّبُعُ إِلَّا مَا ذَكَّيۡتُمۡ وَمَا ذُبِحَ عَلَى ٱلنُّصُبِ وَأَن تَسۡتَقۡسِمُواْ بِٱلۡأَزۡلَٰمِۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ فِسۡقٌۗ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ يَئِسَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مِن دِينِكُمۡ فَلَا تَخۡشَوۡهُمۡ وَٱخۡشَوۡنِۚ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ أَكۡمَلۡتُ لَكُمۡ دِينَكُمۡ وَأَتۡمَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ نِعۡمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلۡإِسۡلَٰمَ دِينࣰ اۚ فَمَنِ ٱضۡطُرَّ فِي مَخۡمَصَةٍ غَيۡرَ مُتَجَانِفࣲ لِّإِثۡمࣲ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
5:3.en: Forbidden unto you (for food) are carrion and blood and swineflesh, and that which hath been dedicated unto any other than Allah, and the strangled, and the dead through beating, and the dead through falling from a height, and that which hath been killed by (the goring of) horns, and the devoured of wild beasts, saving that which ye make lawful (by the death-stroke), and that which hath been immolated unto idols. And (forbidden is it) that ye swear by the divining arrows. This is an abomination. This day are those who disbelieve in despair of (ever harming) your religion; so fear them not, fear Me! This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion al-Islam. Whoso is forced by hunger, not by will, to sin: (for him) lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

40:28.ar: وَقَالَ رَجُلࣱ مُّؤۡمِنࣱ مِّنۡ ءَالِ فِرۡعَوۡنَ يَكۡتُمُ إِيمَٰنَهُۥٓ أَتَقۡتُلُونَ رَجُلًا أَن يَقُولَ رَبِّيَ ٱللَّهُ وَقَدۡ جَآءَكُم بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ مِن رَّبِّكُمۡۖ وَإِن يَكُ كَٰذِبࣰ ا فَعَلَيۡهِ كَذِبُهُۥۖ وَإِن يَكُ صَادِقࣰ ا يُصِبۡكُم بَعۡضُ ٱلَّذِي يَعِدُكُمۡۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي مَنۡ هُوَ مُسۡرِفࣱ كَذَّابࣱ‏
40:28.en: And a believing man of Pharaoh's family, who hid his faith, said: Would ye kill a man because he saith: My Lord is Allah, and hath brought you clear proofs from your Lord? If he is lying, then his lie is upon him; and if he is truthful, then some of that wherewith he threateneth you will strike you. Lo! Allah guideth not one who is a prodigal, a liar

41:37.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِ ٱلَّيۡلُ وَٱلنَّهَارُ وَٱلشَّمۡسُ وَٱلۡقَمَرُۚ لَا تَسۡجُدُواْ لِلشَّمۡسِ وَلَا لِلۡقَمَرِ وَٱسۡجُدُواْۤ لِلَّهِۤ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَهُنَّ إِن كُنتُمۡ إِيَّاهُ تَعۡبُدُونَ
41:37.en: And of His portents are the night and the day and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or the moon; but prostrate to Allah Who created them, if it is in truth Him Whom ye worship

41:38.ar: فَإِنِ ٱسۡتَكۡبَرُواْ فَٱلَّذِينَ عِندَ رَبِّكَ يُسَبِّحُونَ لَهُۥ بِٱلَّيۡلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ وَهُمۡ لَا يَسۡـَٔمُونَ۩
41:38.en: But if they are too proud - still those who are with thy Lord glorify Him night and day, and tire not

Q7HS2yRbOr4.speaker: adnan
Q7HS2yRbOr4.speaker_note: Ramadan Quranic Themes series on his channel; speaks as the imam about his own dawah and the London community
Q7HS2yRbOr4.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 23: Sincere Da'wah
Q7HS2yRbOr4.one_line: Dawah is every Muslim's obligation and must be sincere and agenda-free, shown by the believer of Pharaoh's family, the Prophet's reply to Utbah, and good deeds.
Q7HS2yRbOr4.summary: He calls dawah the main function of a Muslim community and insists on sincerity: dawah with strings attached, seeking loyalty to a group or party, becomes a transaction. True dawah is a gift offered for Allah's sake, the mission of the prophets now shared by every Muslim within their capacity, mostly through practice rather than preaching. He laments that London's Muslims do little organised outreach: of roughly 40,000, only a fraction appear even at Eid, imams reach only those in the masjid, and converts are poorly supported. From 40:38-45 he presents the believer of Pharaoh's family, who addressed his people as 'my people' out of love and risked his life for their salvation, and notes Ali's judgment that Abu Bakr, beaten senseless defending the Prophet, was even braver. From 41:6 and 41:13 he tells how Quraysh sent Utbah to offer the Prophet wealth, women and kingship, and how he listened patiently, then recited that he wanted nothing but to call them to one God. From 41:33 he concludes that the best speech is calling to Allah through good deeds, since actions speak louder than words, while still declaring oneself Muslim.

outline.heading: Dawah as the community's main function
outline.gist: The Muslim goal is to increase guidance; dawah needs finesse, knowledge and commitment and takes many forms, his own being mostly verbal and directed at Muslims.

outline.heading: Sincerity: dawah without strings
outline.gist: Without sincerity dawah becomes agenda-driven, seeking loyalty, support for a cause, or membership of a group or party.

outline.heading: A gift, not a transaction
outline.gist: Offer the guidance and keep walking; if you expect something back, say so openly as a transaction and let the person decline.

outline.heading: Bringing Allah's lost servants back to Him
outline.gist: Dawah done for Allah's sake is the most valuable act, the sole mission of the prophets, and that burden is now spread across all Muslims.

outline.heading: Most dawah is practice, not preaching
outline.gist: His lectures are under two percent of dawah; most happens through conduct among friends, work, school and family. Do not embellish Islam to impress people; it is already perfected.

outline.heading: Outreach among the five community focuses
outline.gist: Of education, mentorship, advocacy, financial centralisation and outreach, outreach to Muslims outside the masjid and to non-Muslims is the one done worst.

outline.heading: Where are 25,000 of London's Muslims?
outline.gist: Around 40,000 Muslims live in the city, yet perhaps 4,000 attend the last ten nights, 7,000 Eid and 15,000 the Eid market; we do not know who the rest are or what they need.

outline.heading: Imams' reach ends at the masjid door
outline.gist: Even online content reaches only those who already know the centre; organised efforts must go into schools, universities and workplaces, where Muslim students fill Jumuah halls.

outline.heading: Converts left without a new family
outline.gist: Converts lose relatives and social circles, and the community does not yet become their family.

outline.heading: The believer of Pharaoh's family
outline.gist: He empathised with the Children of Israel, helped Musa escape, and spoke out when the plotting to kill Musa began.

outline.heading: 'O my people': belonging, not ownership
outline.gist: His repeated 'my people' expressed love and belonging, wanting them spared suffering.

outline.heading: Brief enjoyment and the lasting home
outline.gist: This life is passing enjoyment, the Hereafter is the abode; evil is repaid in kind while believers' good is rewarded beyond reckoning.

outline.heading: 'I call you to salvation and you call me to the Fire'
outline.gist: He calls them to the Mighty, the Forgiving, warns they will remember his words, and entrusts his fate to Allah, knowing they may kill him.

outline.heading: Allah protected him
outline.gist: He survived the plots while Pharaoh's people drowned, and stayed in Egypt carrying on Musa's legacy.

outline.heading: Ali: Abu Bakr was braver
outline.gist: Asked who was bravest, Ali named Abu Bakr, who unlike the hidden believer openly pushed back those assaulting the Prophet with the same words.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr beaten senseless for the Prophet
outline.gist: Beaten until his face was swollen flat, his first words on waking were about the Prophet, and he had his daughters carry him to see him.

outline.heading: Sincere dawah seeks their salvation, not your tally
outline.gist: It is not about counting converts or personal accomplishment but about love for the people and for their Lord.

outline.heading: 'I am only a human like you'
outline.gist: The Prophet's only distinction is revelation that God is one; walk straight to Him and seek His forgiveness.

outline.heading: Why Quraysh wanted a deal
outline.gist: His message threatened their religious and financial tyranny, so the elite hoped to buy him into their ranks.

outline.heading: Wealth, women, kingship or a healer
outline.gist: Utbah offered him the greatest fortune, the most beautiful wives, rule over them, or treatment if he was possessed.

outline.heading: The Prophet lets him finish
outline.gist: He listened in silence, asked whether Utbah was done, and replied only by reciting the Quran.

outline.heading: No agenda: one God and an uncorrupted path
outline.gist: He wants nothing they own; they must abandon shirk and seek forgiveness for selling religion and treating Allah's laws as negotiable for a price.

outline.heading: The thunderbolt warning and Utbah's hand
outline.gist: At the warning of a punishment like that of 'Ad and Thamud, Utbah clamped his hand over the Prophet's mouth begging him to stop, then let him finish to the verse of prostration.

outline.heading: Utbah returns with a different face
outline.gist: He urged Quraysh to leave the Prophet alone, was mocked, withdrew, and died at Badr without accepting Islam.

outline.heading: Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah?
outline.gist: The verse praises calling to Allah by doing good: actions speak louder than words and are the basis of judgment.

outline.heading: Words contradicted by actions do harm
outline.gist: Someone who says 'I love you' while abusing you is worse than honest hatred; it is how deep trauma is produced in children.

outline.heading: Spouses, words and deeds
outline.gist: Women tend to need to hear love, men to show it through work and provision; both are needed, which is why the verse ends with a spoken declaration.

outline.heading: One good deed outweighs a million lessons
outline.gist: A single moment of ethical conduct can bring more people to Allah than a lifetime of his lectures.

outline.heading: Act, and still say 'I am one of the Muslims'
outline.gist: The best spoken person may say nothing and call through deeds, but should still state plainly who they are.

outline.heading: An obligation on every person
outline.gist: Dawah is not only the imam's job; everyone must do it within their capacity, even if only through behaviour, which carries more reward and impact.

3:142.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتُمۡ أَن تَدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَعۡلَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ جَٰهَدُواْ مِنكُمۡ وَيَعۡلَمَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ
3:142.en: Or deemed ye that ye would enter paradise while yet Allah knoweth not those of you who really strive, nor knoweth those (of you) who are steadfast

2:214.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتُمۡ أَن تَدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَأۡتِكُم مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ خَلَوۡاْ مِن قَبۡلِكُمۖ مَّسَّتۡهُمُ ٱلۡبَأۡسَآءُ وَٱلضَّرَّآءُ وَزُلۡزِلُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَقُولَ ٱلرَّسُولُ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مَعَهُۥ مَتَىٰ نَصۡرُ ٱللَّهِۗ أَلَآ إِنَّ نَصۡرَ ٱللَّهِ قَرِيبࣱ‏
2:214.en: Or think ye that ye will enter paradise while yet there hath not come unto you the like of (that which came to) those who passed away before you? Affliction and adversity befell them, they were shaken as with earthquake, till the messenger (of Allah) and those who believed along with him said: When cometh Allah's help? Now surely Allah's help is nigh

5:21.ar: يَٰقَوۡمِ ٱدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ ٱلۡمُقَدَّسَةَ ٱلَّتِي كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡ وَلَا تَرۡتَدُّواْ عَلَىٰٓ أَدۡبَارِكُمۡ فَتَنقَلِبُواْ خَٰسِرِينَ
5:21.en: O my people! Go into the holy land which Allah hath ordained for you. Turn not in flight, for surely ye turn back as losers

5:22.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰمُوسَىٰٓ إِنَّ فِيهَا قَوۡمࣰ ا جَبَّارِينَ وَإِنَّا لَن نَّدۡخُلَهَا حَتَّىٰ يَخۡرُجُواْ مِنۡهَا فَإِن يَخۡرُجُواْ مِنۡهَا فَإِنَّا دَٰخِلُونَ
5:22.en: They said: O Moses! Lo! a giant people (dwell) therein and lo! we go not in till they go forth from thence. When they go forth from thence, then we will enter (not till then)

5:23.ar: قَالَ رَجُلَانِ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخَافُونَ أَنۡعَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡهِمَا ٱدۡخُلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡبَابَ فَإِذَا دَخَلۡتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمۡ غَٰلِبُونَۚ وَعَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَتَوَكَّلُوٓاْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
5:23.en: Then out spake two of those who feared (their Lord, men) unto whom Allah had been gracious: Enter in upon them by the gate, for if ye enter by it, lo! ye will be victorious. So put your trust (in Allah) if ye are indeed believers

5:24.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰمُوسَىٰٓ إِنَّا لَن نَّدۡخُلَهَآ أَبَدࣰ ا مَّا دَامُواْ فِيهَا فَٱذۡهَبۡ أَنتَ وَرَبُّكَ فَقَٰتِلَآ إِنَّا هَٰهُنَا قَٰعِدُونَ
5:24.en: They said: O Moses! We will never enter (the land) while they are in it. So go thou and thy Lord and fight! We will sit here

110:2.ar: وَرَأَيۡتَ ٱلنَّاسَ يَدۡخُلُونَ فِي دِينِ ٱللَّهِ أَفۡوَاجࣰ ا
110:2.en: And thou seest mankind entering the religion of Allah in troops

47:38.ar: هَٰٓأَنتُمۡ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ تُدۡعَوۡنَ لِتُنفِقُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَمِنكُم مَّن يَبۡخَلُۖ وَمَن يَبۡخَلۡ فَإِنَّمَا يَبۡخَلُ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦۚ وَٱللَّهُ ٱلۡغَنِيُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلۡفُقَرَآءُۚ وَإِن تَتَوَلَّوۡاْ يَسۡتَبۡدِلۡ قَوۡمًا غَيۡرَكُمۡ ثُمَّ لَا يَكُونُوٓاْ أَمۡثَٰلَكُم
47:38.en: Lo! ye are those who are called to spend in the way of Allah, yet among you there are some who hoard. And as for him who hoardeth, he hoardeth only from his soul. And Allah is the Rich, and ye are the poor. And if ye turn away He will exchange you for some other folk, and they will not be the likes of you

5:26.ar: قَالَ فَإِنَّهَا مُحَرَّمَةٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡۛ أَرۡبَعِينَ سَنَةࣰۛ يَتِيهُونَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ فَلَا تَأۡسَ عَلَى ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
5:26.en: (Their Lord) said: For this the land will surely be forbidden them for forty years that they will wander in the earth, bewildered. So grieve not over the wrongdoing folk

k98vp0zBRRE.title: Ramadan Reminders 1446: Victory Is Not a Handout
k98vp0zBRRE.one_line: On the anniversary of the conquest of Mecca, as Gaza's bombing resumes: victory costs effort, unity and sacrifice, and dua alone is not enough.
k98vp0zBRRE.summary: Given on the 20th or 21st of Ramadan 1446, the anniversary of the conquest of Mecca and days after the bombing of Gaza resumed, this khutbah tries to make sense of an ummah weaker and more divided than at any point he can find in its history, watching children pulled from rubble in real time while the world looks away. Change, he insists, must begin deep inside each person and in how Muslims value one another, and the last ten nights are the time to start. The conquest is his model: it came after twenty-one years of effort through Badr, Uhud, the Trench, murdered teachers and the discipline of Hudaybiyyah, and the Prophet entered with his head bowed, turning Sa'd's day of slaughter into a day of mercy. Citing the Quran's repeated question of whether people expected Paradise without being tested, and Bani Israel's refusal to enter the Holy Land, he calls asking for victory while doing nothing, and while fighting over details, a lack of adab; less than one percent of Muslims are working, as he saw in Syria. Victory in Islam means people entering the faith in multitudes. If this generation is passed over, invest in the next. The second khutbah urges the Prophet's practice in the last ten nights and putting Allah's command before oneself.

outline.heading: Opening
Back on the minbar: an unprecedented weakness
outline.gist: Fifteen months on he must again make sense of events in the Holy Land. He knows the ummah's dark periods, but cannot find one with this degree of weakness, division and lack of voice; earlier ones had their own geopolitical and technological reasons.

outline.heading: Now we watch in real time
outline.gist: Past disasters struck distant states, and news arrived after it was over. Today we watch children pulled from rubble and people breathing their last on hospital floors with our own eyes.

outline.heading: A world that chooses to look away
outline.gist: The whole world sees it too and consciously turns a blind eye, whether from fear of the perpetrator or because the victims are valued so little. This cannot be our future; things must change.

outline.heading: Change begins deep inside
outline.gist: Change on a global scale must start in the depths of each person's consciousness and then in communities, until sixty thousand killed in a land smaller than London can no longer be justified.

outline.heading: If we do not value one another, no one will
outline.gist: Four hundred killed in a day while the world carries on trading cannot be acceptable. It begins with Muslims valuing, respecting and loving each other, and there is no better time than Ramadan's last ten nights.

outline.heading: The conquest of Mecca: returning differently
outline.gist: On the 20th or 21st of Ramadan, 8 AH, the Prophet returned to Mecca, no longer entering under conditions imposed on him but reclaiming it from those who held it by oppression.

outline.heading: Everyone wants the victory, few pay for it
outline.gist: We make dua for such a moment but will not put in the work. It does not come without tears, sweat and blood and millions devoting their lives to a cause bigger than themselves.

outline.heading: Entering Mecca with his head bowed
outline.gist: The conquest came after twenty-one years of lifelong effort. At sixty he entered with his face lowered to his camel's neck, overwhelmed by his Lord's generosity, the epitome of humility.

outline.heading: A day of mercy, not slaughter
outline.gist: When Sa'd ibn Ubadah declared it the day of slaughter, the Prophet took the banner from him, called it the day of mercy in which Quraysh would find its honour under Islam, and handed the banner to Sa'd's son.

outline.heading: Name the weakness before seeking solutions
outline.gist: Only when a two-billion-strong ummah spread over every continent admits how divided and weak it is can it begin talking about solutions.

outline.heading: Diversity without tokenism
outline.gist: Institutions manufacture diversity and put one face on a billboard. This masjid holds twenty-seven or twenty-eight nationalities effortlessly, the legacy of a Prophet who brought the message to all humanity.

outline.heading: Straight lines: no one stands ahead
outline.gist: Age, gender, wealth, status, culture and lineage make no difference in salah. No one may stand an inch ahead of the line, and no one may see himself as better.

outline.heading: What did you do with my ummah?
outline.gist: Real unity lives in the heart and puts the ummah's interest above your own agenda. Prepare an answer for when the Prophet asks what you did with the nation he left, rather than living in silos.

outline.heading: An annoying reminder: no going back to normal
outline.gist: Gaza keeps reminding us we cannot just enjoy quiet worship; just as we thought it had stopped, it resumed. The companions in Madinah also grew comfortable with the Prophet leading them in prayer.

outline.heading: From the caravan to the Trench
outline.gist: The Prophet told them there was much more work. The caravan sparked one struggle after another, Badr, Uhud and more, and before the conquest they shivered in cold and fear for days at the Trench.

outline.heading: Treachery, rumours and obedience
outline.gist: Muslims were betrayed, seventy teachers were murdered at Bi'r Ma'unah, and they faced social tests of rumours, military tests and a test of obedience when told to turn back at Hudaybiyyah.

outline.heading: Nothing comes for free
outline.gist: By the time you reach a goal the effort has shown its price. What comes too early is not valued, like wealth handed to the young; Allah grants the outcome after you put in the hours.

outline.heading: Did you think you would enter Paradise? (3:142)
outline.gist: Victory is not a handout. Allah asks again and again whether people expected Paradise, the ultimate triumph, before He exposed who would strive and persevere.

outline.heading: Shaken until they asked when help would come (2:214)
outline.gist: Earlier believers were shaken by psychological and religious earthquakes until even the Prophet among them asked when Allah's help would come. Help is near; the question is who will pay the price.

outline.heading: Dua alone is a lack of adab
outline.gist: Make dua for the people of Gaza, but if that is all, it misunderstands our role: Allah told us to care for the ummah, and we ask Him to do it for us. Musa told Bani Israel simply to enter the gate of Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Go, you and your Lord (5:21-24)
outline.gist: They replied that they would never go in: let Musa and his Lord fight and call them once it was won. We do the same when we raise our hands and do nothing, while actively dividing the ummah.

outline.heading: Less than one percent are working
outline.gist: We tear the ummah's fabric over tertiary details. Two billion people working at full strength could not produce this; less than one percent are working while the rest wait for different news on television.

outline.heading: Waiting for breaking news
outline.gist: He watched it in Syria: people did nothing but sat in front of Al Jazeera every Friday hoping to hear the regime had fallen. It took fifteen years, a million dead and countless drowned in the Mediterranean.

outline.heading: What victory means in Islam
outline.gist: It does not come cheap. Fath is not conquest but strength that draws people into Allah's religion in multitudes (110:2); our victory is people finding guidance.

outline.heading: Our weakness withholds guidance
outline.gist: Weakness lets children freeze barefoot and burn in their sleep, and it holds Allah's guidance back from others. Turn away and He will replace you with a people unlike you (47:38).

outline.heading: The forty years of wandering (5:26)
outline.gist: Allah lost hope in that generation and made them wander forty years until they died; not one of those who refused entered Jerusalem with Yusha'. He fears we are in that moment.

outline.heading: At least invest in the next generation
outline.gist: If Allah judges this generation not worth it and lets it live aimlessly, make sure you invest in the next one, so something comes after you.

outline.heading: Interlude
No more part-time commitment
outline.gist: No time of year is more blessed than the last ten nights. While asking Allah to change you inside, intend to change outside: His command and the Prophet's teaching first, your family next, yourself after. That is what submission means, and its fulfilment is found nowhere else.

outline.heading: Do what the Prophet did in the last ten nights
outline.gist: He let his family sleep through earlier Ramadan nights if they wished, but in the last ten he rolled up his sleeves, prayed most of the night and knocked on their doors to wake them.

outline.heading: The harder it is, the greater the reward
outline.gist: Tired, sleep-deprived and dehydrated, you gain more for the difficulty. He prays that Laylat al-Qadr becomes the beginning of change in the ummah.

outline.heading: Outro

18:9.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتَ أَنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡكَهۡفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُواْ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا عَجَبًا
18:9.en: Or deemest thou that the People of the Cave and the Inscription are a wonder among Our portents

10:90.ar: ۞وَجَٰوَزۡنَا بِبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱلۡبَحۡرَ فَأَتۡبَعَهُمۡ فِرۡعَوۡنُ وَجُنُودُهُۥ بَغۡيࣰ ا وَعَدۡوًاۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَدۡرَكَهُ ٱلۡغَرَقُ قَالَ ءَامَنتُ أَنَّهُۥ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِيٓ ءَامَنَتۡ بِهِۦ بَنُوٓاْ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ وَأَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلۡمُسۡلِمِينَ
10:90.en: And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh with his hosts pursued them in rebellion and transgression, till, when the (fate of) drowning overtook him, he exclaimed: I believe that there is no Allah save Him in Whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who surrender (unto Him)

10:91.ar: ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ وَقَدۡ عَصَيۡتَ قَبۡلُ وَكُنتَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُفۡسِدِينَ
10:91.en: What! Now! When hitherto thou hast rebelled and been of the wrong-doers

4:135.ar: ۞يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ كُونُواْ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلۡقِسۡطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ أَوِ ٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ وَٱلۡأَقۡرَبِينَۚ إِن يَكُنۡ غَنِيًّا أَوۡ فَقِيرࣰ ا فَٱللَّهُ أَوۡلَىٰ بِهِمَاۖ فَلَا تَتَّبِعُواْ ٱلۡهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعۡدِلُواْۚ وَإِن تَلۡوُۥٓاْ أَوۡ تُعۡرِضُواْ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣰ ا
4:135.en: O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred, whether (the case be of) a rich man or a poor man, for Allah is nearer unto both (them ye are). So follow not passion lest ye lapse (from truth) and if ye lapse or fall away, then lo! Allah is ever Informed of what ye do

18:17.ar: ۞وَتَرَى ٱلشَّمۡسَ إِذَا طَلَعَت تَّزَٰوَرُ عَن كَهۡفِهِمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَت تَّقۡرِضُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ وَهُمۡ فِي فَجۡوَةࣲ مِّنۡهُۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۗ مَن يَهۡدِ ٱللَّهُ فَهُوَ ٱلۡمُهۡتَدِۖ وَمَن يُضۡلِلۡ فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ وَلِيࣰّ ا مُّرۡشِدࣰ ا
18:17.en: And thou mightest have seen the sun when it rose move away from their cave to the right, and when it set go past them on the left, and they were in the cleft thereof. That was (one) of the portents of Allah. He whom Allah guideth, he indeed is led aright, and he whom He sendeth astray, for him thou wilt not find a guiding friend

18:14.ar: وَرَبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ إِذۡ قَامُواْ فَقَالُواْ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَن نَّدۡعُوَاْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَٰهࣰ اۖ لَّقَدۡ قُلۡنَآ إِذࣰ ا شَطَطًا
18:14.en: And We made firm their hearts when they stood forth and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We cry unto no Allah beside Him, for then should we utter an enormity

18:13.ar: نَّحۡنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيۡكَ نَبَأَهُم بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ إِنَّهُمۡ فِتۡيَةٌ ءَامَنُواْ بِرَبِّهِمۡ وَزِدۡنَٰهُمۡ هُدࣰ ى
18:13.en: We narrate unto thee their story with truth. Lo! they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance

18:19.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ بَعَثۡنَٰهُمۡ لِيَتَسَآءَلُواْ بَيۡنَهُمۡۚ قَالَ قَآئِلࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡۖ قَالُواْ لَبِثۡنَا يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمࣲۚ قَالُواْ رَبُّكُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثۡتُمۡ فَٱبۡعَثُوٓاْ أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمۡ هَٰذِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ فَلۡيَنظُرۡ أَيُّهَآ أَزۡكَىٰ طَعَامࣰ ا فَلۡيَأۡتِكُم بِرِزۡقࣲ مِّنۡهُ وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ وَلَا يُشۡعِرَنَّ بِكُمۡ أَحَدًا
18:19.en: And in like manner We awakened them that they might question one another. A speaker from among them said: How long have ye tarried? They said: We have tarried a day or some part of a day, (Others) said: Your Lord best knoweth what ye have tarried. Now send one of you with this your silver coin unto the city, and let him see what food is purest there and bring you a supply thereof. Let him be courteous and let no man know of you
